SPARe: Stacked Parallelism with Adaptive Reordering
for Fault-Tolerant LLM Pretraining Systems with 100​k+100\mathrm{k}+ GPUs

Jin Lee Affiliation: Department of ECE, University of California, Santa Barbara, United States Affiliation: Argonne National Laboratory, Illinois, United States Correspondence to: hojin@ucsb.edu    Zhonghao Chen Affiliation: Department of ECE, University of Florida, United States    Xuhang He Affiliation: Department of ECE, University of Florida, United States    Robert Underwood Affiliation: Argonne National Laboratory, Illinois, United States    Bogdan Nicolae Affiliation: Argonne National Laboratory, Illinois, United States    Franck Cappello Affiliation: Argonne National Laboratory, Illinois, United States    Xiaoyi Lu Affiliation: Department of ECE, University of Florida, United States    Sheng Di Affiliation: Argonne National Laboratory, Illinois, United States Correspondence to: sdi1@anl.gov    Zheng Zhang Affiliation: Department of ECE, University of California, Santa Barbara, United States Correspondence to: zhengzhang@ece.ucsb.edu
Abstract

In large-scale LLM pretraining systems with 100​k+100\mathrm{k}+ GPUs, failures become the norm rather than the exception, and restart costs can dominate wall-clock training time. However, existing fault-tolerance mechanisms are largely unprepared for this restart-dominant regime. To address this challenge, we propose SPARe—Stacked Parallelism with Adaptive Reordering—a fault-tolerance framework that masks node failures during gradient synchronization by stacking redundant data shards across parallelism groups and adaptively reordering execution. SPARe achieves availability comparable to traditional replication while maintaining near-constant computation overhead of only 2∼3×2\sim 3\times, even under high redundancy where traidional replication would require linearly inflating overhead. We derive closed-form expressions for endurable failure count and computation overhead, validate them via SimGrid-based discrete-event simulation, and jointly optimize redundancy and checkpointing to minimize time-to-train. At extreme scale with up to 600​k600\mathrm{k} GPUs, SPARe reduces time-to-train by 40∼50%40\sim 50\% compared to traditional replication.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

The industrial high-performance computing (HPC) system has scaled up to over 100​k+100\mathrm{k}+ GPUs to meet the computing demand of large-scale pre-training of AI foundation models. As the number of GPUs (#​GPU\#\mathrm{GPU}) increases, the mean time between failures (MTBF) of system decreases as 𝒪⁡(1#​GPU)\mathcal{O}(\frac{1}{\#\mathrm{GPU}}) (Kokolis et al., 2025; Ostrouchov et al., 2020). Meanwhile, upon system failures, the restarting latency inflates quadratically or worse by default due to global collectives initialization and synchronization (Jiang et al., 2024; Si et al., 2025). As a result, cumulative waste of system downtime from frequent failures grows rapidly, leading to lower system availability11 1 Fraction of time the system is operational: uptime divided by total wall-clock time (Avizienis et al., 2004). and longer time-to-train22 2 Total wall-clock time of training. Job Completion Time.. The LlaMa-3 paper (Dubey et al., 2024) (Section 3.3.4) reports that the average failure rate is around 44 interruptions per 10001000 servers (8 GPUs per server) per day. This corresponds to one failure every three hours on average for a 16​k16\mathrm{k} H100-GPU system. Extrapolating using the empirically validated MTBF scaling model in Kokolis et al. (2025), failures would occur every 30 minutes at 96​k96\mathrm{k} GPUs and every five minutes at 600​k600\mathrm{k} GPUs. This projection is already harsh, yet still optimistic, as modern pretraining systems are increasingly heterogeneous, which further exacerbates failure rates (Jones, 2020; Jayaram Subramanya et al., 2023).

As failure-induced global restarts now happen once per hour or more, collective communication (re)initialization once neglected now dominates runtime. At 96​k96\mathrm{k} GPUs, Si et al. (2025) show that NCCL​_​init\mathrm{NCCL\_init} and similar routines become a major bottleneck; even after optimization (Jiang et al., 2024; Si et al., 2025), key collectives still scale linearly with #​GPU\#\mathrm{GPU}. Hu et al. (2025) similarly report that large messages throughput in NCCL is best with linear-scaling algorithms. As a result, restart latency is projected to grow linearly with #​GPU\#\mathrm{GPU} while MTBF shrinks inversely, pushing LLM pretraining system towards a restart-dominant regime where expected restart latency prevails over useful work time. For example, a 600​k+600\mathrm{k}+ cluster of 55-min MTBF may spend ≥60\geq 60-min on global restart after every failure. To address this challenge, three major approaches have been considered to achieve fault-tolerance in distributed training: checkpointing, partial recovery, and replication.

Checkpointing attempts to minimize rework burden from progress loss by failures. Universal checkpointing (Lian et al., 2025) decouples checkpoint state from a fixed parallelism configuration to enable flexible and fast recovery. GEMINI (Wang et al., 2023) maintains lightweight in-memory snapshots for near-instant rollback. Just-in-Time checkpointing (Gupta et al., 2024) adapts snapshot timing to high risk windows. Oobleck (Jang et al., 2023) reduces replay cost in pipeline parallelism (Huang et al., 2019) by replaying short segments. Multi-level checkpointing (Di et al., 2014; Maurya et al., 2024; Maurya et al., 2026) amortizes I/O across device, host, and storage tiers. These advances lighten the rework burden once the system is back on the job. In the restart-dominant regime, however, the performance bottleneck shifts to restart downtime: the cumulative waste spent before the system can resume the job. In this setting, reducing the number of global restarts becomes critical to improving system availability hence reducing time-to-train.

In parallel, traditional replication methods have been revisited to improve availability by masking failures with redundant computation, and partial recovery has been proposed to replace global restarts with cheaper, local system recoveries (Losada et al., 2020). Ferreira et al. (2011) disclosed that even minimal redundancy r=2r=2 can tolerate a large number of failures and Benoit et al. (2019) proposed an optimized strategy to minimize time-to-train with checkpointing. However, replication is constrained by a fundamental ceiling: degree-rr replication incurs r×r\times more computation, which becomes prohibitive in practice. This strongly motivates the need for a direct yet practical approach to improving availability without extravagant waste, especially as we are at the doorstep of the restart-dominant regime.

We hereby propose SPARe: Stacked Parallelism with Adaptive Reordering, a failure-masking scheme as effective as traditional replication yet pays only near-constant overhead around 2∼3×2\sim 3\times even for high redundancy like r∼20r\sim 20. Instead of fully replicating computation, SPARe stacks shards of computation across synchronous Data Parallelism (Zinkevich et al., 2010; Sergeev and Del Balso, 2018) so that redundant workload can be minimized by adaptively reordering the stacks. Also, SPARe is orthogonal to progress loss rework hence can seamlessly merge with any checkpointing scheme. Our contributions in this work are:

  • •

    We derive working formulas for the expected failure count and computation overhead SPARe endures and pays, and validate them with our simulation results.

  • •

    We optimize SPARe with checkpointing (SPARe+CKPT) to find optimal redundancy rr to minimize time-to-train.

  • •

    Lastly, we provide discrete-event simulations using SimGrid (Casanova et al., 2014) (a widely used large parallel system simulation toolkit) and with realistic system parameters for a 600​k600\mathrm{k} H100 cluster to benchmark SPARe+CKPT against traditional replication with checkpointing (Rep+CKPT) and checkpointing only (CKPT-only), showing 40∼50%40\sim 50\% gain in time-to-train.

2 Background

2.1 Synchronous Data Parallelism

Fig. 1 shows synchronous Data Parallelism (Zinkevich et al., 2010; Sergeev and Del Balso, 2018): the system consists of N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} identical GPU groups, and the total training data is divided into NN equal-size shards with index i∈[N]:={0,1,…,N−1}i\in[N]:=\{0,1,\dots,N-1\}, each distributed to the group of the same index. Each group holds an identical copy of the entire model parameters; hence, group size is decided by the size of the model to train. Based on recent trends in scaling (Dubey et al., 2024; Chu et al., 2025) it would be reasonable to assume that the size is hundreds to a few thousands. Hence, in this work we set N∼102−3N\sim 10^{2-3}. Each group deploys a complex parallelism topology (Shoeybi et al., 2019), so a failed node (GPU) stops the entire group.

At each training step, group ii computes a partial gradient 𝐠i\mathbf{g}_{i} from its shard ii. After all groups are done computing their own partial gradients, the system communicator triggers global all-reduce collectives to aggregate them into the full gradient 𝐠¯=1N​∑j=1N𝐠i\overline{\mathbf{g}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\mathbf{g}_{i}, and distributes 𝐠¯\overline{\mathbf{g}} back to all groups for model updates. Hence, all NN types of {𝐠i}\{\mathbf{g}_{i}\} must be collectible for the system to finish one training step: every single loss of any of the group stops training.

2.2 Node Failures in Large Parallel HPC System

In large GPU clusters, node failures occur when nodes are forcibly lost by fail-stop faults such as GPU memory error, driver/kernel faults, process crash, power/thermal excursions and etc., and the aggregate failure rate rises with #​GPU\#\mathrm{GPU} (Schroeder and Gibson, 2009). Kokolis et al. (2025) empirically validated that MTBF decreases by ∝1#​GPU\propto\frac{1}{\#\mathrm{GPU}} for jobs with more than 3232 GPUs. As MTBF decreases, time wasted outside of training increases, hence the total wall-clock time to finish training also increases.

The well-known Young & Daly’s formula (Young, 1974; Daly, 2006) gives optimal checkpointing period that minimizes the time to finish training when the rework waste on lost progress is the primary bottleneck. However, in restart-dominant regime, system downtime is of main concern; in this setting minimizing the portion of the downtime, hence maximizing the system availability, leads to the minimal time to finish training. For system failure interval TfT_{f}, checkpointing period TcT_{c}, checkpoint save time TsT_{s}, and global restart cost TrT_{r}, recent work of Saxena et al. (2024) gives optimal checkpointing period for maximal availability as:

Tc⋆=Ts+Ts2+2​Ts​(Tf+Tr),,T_{c}^{\star}=T_{s}+\sqrt{T_{s}^{2}+2\,T_{s}\,(T_{f}+T_{r})},, (1)

where corresponding maximal system availability is:

A⋆​(Tf,Ts,Tc⋆,Tr)=Tf−Tf​TsTc⋆Tf+Tc⋆2+Tr.A^{\star}(T_{f},T_{s},T^{\star}_{c},T_{r})=\frac{T_{f}-\frac{T_{f}T_{s}}{T^{\star}_{c}}}{T_{f}+\frac{T^{\star}_{c}}{2}+T_{r}}. (2)

In our work TrT_{r}, TsT_{s} are fixed parameters decided by model size and system capacity, while TfT_{f} is a design factor decided by redundancy rr for given budget NN. Hence we denote Tc⋆T_{c}^{\star} and A⋆A^{\star} as functions of TfT_{f}: Tc⋆​(Tf)T_{c}^{\star}(T_{f}), A⋆​(Tf)A^{\star}(T_{f}).

2.3 Partial Recovery: Avoiding Global Restart

Partial recovery minimizes downtime by localizing recovery across surviving nodes so that system can resume job without going through the costly global restart (Bland et al., 2013). For example, (1) communicator shrinking excludes failed nodes (nodes) from the job and forms a new communicator over the survivors (Losada et al., 2020; , 2025), (2) Non-shrinking replacement respawns failed nodes or activates hot spares to merge them back in (Losada et al., 2020), (3) Rollback with message logging restarts only the failed nodes from a checkpoint and uses logged/replayed messages to restore a consistent global state (Elnozahy et al., 2002), (4) Runtime reinitialization rebuilds runtime and communicator state through the batch system (Georgakoudis et al., 2020), and (5) Task migration dynamically remaps failed work units onto healthy resources (Chakravorty et al., 2006).

In this paper, we consider shrinking paired with replication or checkpointing as the default partial recovery, as it is fastest at re-establishing collective communication across surviving groups and also directly supported by NCCL (, 2025), PyTorch (, 2024), and MPI (Losada et al., 2020). Moreover, Bland et al. (2015) report shrinking takes tens of milliseconds for hundreds of nodes. As the communicator we need to shrink is the one that aggregates partial gradients, hence of hundreds to a few thousands of nodes, we therefore treat its cost as negligible: we presume the job resumes without any meaningful delay after each failure if partial recovery is available for the gradient synchronization communicator as long as all partial gradients are collectible.

2.4 Traditional Replication: Robust yet Expensive

Fig. 2 shows replication of degree r=3r=3. With partial recovery, system can endure multiple failures without job interruption as long as all types of shards are surviving on the job. However, assuming fixed GPU budget, each group now hosts 3×3\times shards compared to the original Data Parallelism, hence 3×3\times workload if we regard the data size as equivalent to the computation amount for simplicity. Assuming random independent failures, higher redundancy rr masks more failures before depletion (Ferreira et al., 2011), yet also linearly inflates the workload by r×r\times, a prohibitive overhead that degrades time-to-train in practice.

3 SPARe: Stacked Parallelism with Adaptive Reordering

Now we present the SPARe framework. In the imminent restart-dominant regime, one way to improve the system availability (2) to a practical level (OPEN≥90%)\geq 90\%) is to increase the system failure interval TfT_{f}, especially since reducing the global restart cost TrT_{r} below the linear scalability has been revealed to be a very subtle problem (Si et al., 2025; Hu et al., 2025). Traditional replication easily increases TfT_{f} by masking multiple node failures with redundant computation, yet the linearly inflating computation overhead is prohibitive in practice. SPARe aims to answer to this challenge:

Can we mask frequent failures with redundant computation while keeping the overhead down to be near-constant?

Sec. 3.1 introduces the key ideas of SPARe to solve this challenge, and Sec. 3.2 explains the algorithm flow of SPARe.

3.1 Key Ideas of SPARe

Traditional replication requires the groups to compute all assigned data to collect all partial gradients. Key intuition behind SPARe is to replicate shards of computation (data) instead of fully replicating each group, and stack them across parallelism so that all types of partial gradients are collectible before computing all assigned data (stacks) at each group. Below are the key steps of SPARe of redundancy rr:

  • •

    From synchronous Data Parallelism introduced in Sec. 2.1, replicate all NN types of data shards {D0,D1,⋯,DN−1}\{D_{0},D_{1},\cdots,D_{N-1}\} and stack them up to rr stacks with cyclic rotation across parallelism so that all types are present in every stack.

  • •

    At each training step, schedule gradient synchronization right after all types of shards are computed: aggregate partial gradients as soon as all types are collectible.

  • •

    To compute all types of shards within the minimal number of stacks at each training step, reorder the shard stack in each group accordingly to the failure accumulation.

In this way, redundant computation needed to mask failures can be kept down to be minimal at each training step. With judicious scheduling of gradient synchronization and failure-adaptive reordering, SPARe needs to compute only 2∼2.82\sim 2.8 stacks in average to collect all partial gradients at each training step even for high redundancies such as r=20r=20, whereas traditional replication requires to finish computing all r=20r=20 stacks amount of data in every training step.

3.2 Algorithm Flow of SPARe

Before we explain the algorithm flow of SPARe we first define the failure ontology we use throughout this work. We denote an individual GPU failure as a node failure. In Data Parallelism any node failure interrupts the job and enforces global restart. However, for replication and SPARe, global restart occurs only when any shard type ii depletes with failure accumulation: we refer to this incident as the wipe-out of shard ii, and also as system failure. Lastly, we assume the node failures are detected when the system calls all-reduce across parallelism groups for gradient synchronization, following the typical large parallel system convention.

The training loop of SPARe develops on the synchronous Data Parallelism introduced in Sec. 2.1, except that it does not compute all the stacks to complete a training step. Instead, it triggers global all-reduce as soon as a committed number of stacks are computed, which is aimed to be the minimal stacks required to collect all partial gradients so that the redundant computation can be minimized at each step. We denote this committed number as all-reduce stack, which is set as 11 by default when training starts.

When node failure happens, the next all-reduce will fail with collective hang/drop and system will detect the failure. SPARe then initiates the reordering controller, ReCtlr, which serves three purposes:

  • •

    System failure detection;

  • •

    Finding the minimal all-reduce stack for subsequent steps;

  • •

    Reorder stacks accordingly with minimal movement.

If ReCtlr detects system failure, system undergoes global restart, reset the stacks to the original order and the all-reduce stack back to be 11. If not, ReCtlr finds the minimal all-reduce stack with the new failure(s) and reorder the stacks accordingly. After ReCtlr, system needs to collect the missing partial gradients lost by the new failure(s) to complete the current training step, hence commands all surviving groups hosting the missing shard types to compute them. We denote this additional computation stack as patch compute. After patch compute, the system shrinks the communicator to the surviving groups, performs gradient synchronization and model updates, commits the new all-reduce stack and reordered stacks, then proceeds to the next training step. See Alg. (1) for the pseudo-code of the SPARe training loop.

ReCtlr plays the central role in SPARe training loop and it runs with 3 phases:

  • •

    Phase 0 decides if reordering is needed with the new failure(s), by checking if the current all-reduce stack can collect all partial gradients across the surviving groups via Hopcroft-Karp (HK) algorithm (Hopcroft and Karp, 1973) on the fixed stacks of shards; we denote it as HK-Fixed. HK algorithm checks the feasibility of a bipartite graph between NN shard types to the stacks of surviving groups up to the all-reduce stack. If HK-Fixed succeeds, no reordering is needed, hence ReCtlr quits.

  • •

    Phase 1 searches for the minimal all-reduce stack that can collect all partial gradients, by incrementally iterating the HK algorithm from the previous all-reduce stack up to redundancy degree rr, now allowing free permutation of shard stacks within each surviving group (HK-Free). If no HK-Free iteration succeeds, a wipe-out has occurred, and ReCtlr flags a system failure to trigger a global restart.

  • •

    Phase 2 finds how to reorder the stacks with minimal movement to achieve the newly found minimal all-reduce stack, by running min-cost max-flow algorithm (Goldberg and Tarjan, 1990), MCMF.

See Alg. (2) for the pseudo-code of ReCtlr. At N∼102−3N\sim 10^{2-3}, HK-Fixed, HK-Free, and MCMF do not require significant computational cost. See App. D for the detailed descriptions and complexity analysis of ReCtlr.

4 Theoretical Analysis of SPARe

In this Section, we provide theoretical analysis on three key properties of SPARe:

  • •

    How many failures can SPARe endure before wipe-out?

  • •

    How much computation overhead SPARe needs to pay?

  • •

    What is the optimal redundancy for minimal time-to-train when merged with checkpointing?

We provide key results on the first two questions in Sec. 4.1 and show joint optimization with checkpointing in Sec. 4.2. In our theoretical analysis, we assume exponential distribution on node failures (uniform interval). However, we consider the realistic Weibull distribution (Weibull, 1951; Schroeder and Gibson, 2009) in our simulations in Sec. 5.

4.1 Theoretical Results about SPARe

In order to minimize the impact of each individual node failure, we design SPARe so that no pair of different shard types overlap in more than one group as in Fig. 3. See App. B.1 for the shard distribution rule that achieves this goal. In this way, wipe-out incidents of different shard types are almost independent to each other, hence their statistics can be approximated to follow the Poisson distribution (Chen, 1975; Barbour and Eagleson, 1983). This leads to two key results:

  • •

    SPARe can asymptotically endure as many failures as traditional replication: Theorem 4.1.

  • •

    SPARe can achieve computation overhead close to its theoretical lower bound: Theorem 4.2.

Theorem 4.1 (Average Failure Count).

The average failure count μ⁡(N,r)\mu(N,r) SPARe can mask before the first wipe-out is asymptotically:

μ⁡(N,r)≈Γ⁡(1/r)r​N 1−1/r,\mu(N,r)\;\approx\;\boxed{\;\frac{\Gamma(1/r)}{r}\,N^{\,1-1/r}\;}, (3)

where Γ\Gamma refers to the Gamma function in NIST (2025).

Proof.

According to Barbour and Eagleson (1983), wipe-out incidents are almost independent to each other so that Poisson approximation is valid (Chen, 1975):

μ⁡(N,r)\displaystyle\mu(N,r) ≈∑k≥0exp⁡(−N​(kN)r)≈N​∫0∞e−N​tr​𝑑t\displaystyle\approx\sum_{k\geq 0}\exp\Big(-N\Big(\frac{k}{N}\Big)^{r}\Big)\;\approx\;N\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-Nt^{r}}\,dt
=1r​N1−1/r​Γ​(1r)=Γ⁡(1/r)r​N 1−1/r.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{r}N^{1-1/r}\Gamma\!\Big(\frac{1}{r}\Big)\;=\;\frac{\Gamma(1/r)}{r}\,N^{\,1-1/r}.\vskip-10.00002pt (4)

See App. B.2 for the full proof. ∎

μ⁡(N,r)\mu(N,r) derived in (3) is consistent to the traditional replication formula given by (Ferreira et al., 2011). Fig. 4 shows that SPARe can endure up to 426426 failures in average for N=600N=600 with redundancy r=20r=20. This means that for a system of MTBF mm, SPARe effectively increases it up to 426×m426\times m, substantially improving the system availability. Traditional replication requires 20×20\times computation overhead for this availability gain. However, with adaptive reordering, SPARe only pays 2.8×2.8\times for the same availability gain.

Theorem 4.2 (Average Computation Overhead).

The average computation overhead S¯​(N,r)\overline{S}(N,r) SPARe needs to pay before the first wipe-out is approximately

S¯​(N,r)≈1⌊μ⌋​∑k=0⌊μ⌋−1(c⁡(k)+ρk),\overline{S}(N,r)\approx\boxed{\frac{1}{\lfloor\mu\rfloor}\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor\mu\rfloor-1}\ \Big(c(k)+\rho_{k}\Big)}, (5)

where μ\mu is the average failure count of Thm. (4.1) and c⁡(k)c(k) is the lower-bound of all-reduce stack: c⁡(k):=⌈NN−k⌉c(k):=\left\lceil\frac{N}{N-k}\right\rceil. ρk\rho_{k} is the probability of patch compute at kk failures, ρk:=max⁡{0, 2​N−nk}/nk\rho_{k}:=\max\{0,\,2N-n_{k}\}/n_{k}, where nk:=c⁡(k)​(N−k)n_{k}:=c(k)(N-k).

S¯​(N,r)\overline{S}(N,r) has an idealistic lower bound of:

S¯​(N,r)≳1⌊μ⌋​∑k=0⌊μ⌋−1c⁡(k),\overline{S}(N,r)\gtrsim\frac{1}{\lfloor\mu\rfloor}\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor\mu\rfloor-1}c(k), (6)

achievable if system detects failures instantly hence does not require patch computes.

Proof.

Probabilities of adversarial cases where all-reduce stack is forced to be >c⁡(k)>c(k) can be formulated by Hall’s Marriage Theorem (Hall, 1987), which are negligible at N∼102−3N\sim 10^{2-3}. Therefore all-reduce stack ≈c⁡(k)\approx c(k). Expected number of patch compute per step can be approximated by noting that the probability of a random failure hitting any singleton type33 3 Type that is computed only once before all-reduce, hence its loss prevents gradient synchronization. scales as ρk\rho_{k}: Pr⁡(patch compute∣k)≈ρk\Pr(\text{patch compute}\mid k)\approx\rho_{k}. See App. B.3 for the full proof. ∎

Fig. 5 clearly shows that the average computation overhead of SPARe is near-constant around 2∼2.8×2\sim 2.8\times compared to the linearly scaling r×r\times of traditional replication. As SPARe achieves as high availability as replication, near-constant overhead results in significant gain in time-to-train.

See App. C for Monte-Carlo validation on μ⁡(N,r)\mu(N,r) and the lower bound of S¯​(N,r)\overline{S}(N,r), which shows 1.13%1.13\% and 0.60%0.60\% absolute error respectively.

4.2 Joint Optimization with Checkpointing

SPARe cannot mask failures indefinitely hence must be paired with checkpointing to ensure forward progress under continual system failures. Merging two schemes, SPARe+CKPT, entails two coupled trade-offs: one that hinges on checkpointing period, checkpointing overhead versus rework amount, and the other on redundancy rr, availability gains versus computation overhead. In the following, we provide the joint optimization of SPARe+CKPT to find the optimal redundancy rr and corresponding checkpointing period that minimize time-to-train.

Let T0T_{0} be the time-to-train of NN-way Data Parallelism in no failure scenario. Then the useful work time a SPARe needs to finish is T0×S¯​(N,r)T_{0}\times\overline{S}(N,r) . Since system availability (2) is the fraction of useful work time over time-to-train, we can set a normalized time-to-train function J⁡(r)J(r) as:

J⁡(r):=time-to-trainT0=S¯​(N,r)A⋆​(μ​(N,r)​m).J(r):=\frac{\text{time-to-train}}{T_{0}}=\frac{\overline{S}(N,r)}{A^{\star}(\mu(N,r)m)}. (7)

where mm is the system MTBF on node failures.

Theorem 4.3 (Optimal r⋆r^{\star} for minimal time-to-train).

Using checkpointing period of Eq. (1), SPARe+CKPT achieves minimal time-to-train at optimal redundancy r⋆r^{\star}:

r⋆≈⌊log2⁡N+0.833⌋.r^{\star}\approx\boxed{\left\lfloor\log_{2}N+0.833\right\rfloor}. (8)
Proof.

Substitute Eq. (1) (2) (3) (5) to J⁡(r)J(r). J⁡(r)J(r) is minimized around r⋆r^{\star} that satisfies μ⁡(N,r⋆)≈N/2\mu(N,r^{\star})\approx N/2 and S¯​(N,r⋆)≈2\overline{S}(N,r^{\star})\approx 2. Let ε:=1/r⋆\varepsilon:=1/r^{\star} and use Γ⁡(ε)=1ε−γ+O⁡(ε)\Gamma(\varepsilon)=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}-\gamma+O(\varepsilon). Solving it with logarithm yields

r⋆≈log2⁡N+γln⁡2≈log2⁡N+0.833.r^{\star}\;\approx\;\log_{2}N+\frac{\gamma}{\ln 2}\;\approx\;\log_{2}N+0.833.\vskip-5.0pt (9)

See App. B.4 for the full proof. ∎

5 System Performance Evaluation

This section evaluates the performance of SPARe via a solid discrete-event simulation developed based on SimGrid (Casanova et al., 2013) – a state-of-the-art distributed/parallel computing system simulator that facilitates with rigorous emulation of computer networks (Varga, 2001), computer architecture (Binkert et al., 2011), and distributed large-scale systems (Casanova et al., 2008). By modeling the system as a chronology of time-stamped events such as compute, collectives, failure, and advances time by processing the next event rather than by fixed steps (Tocher and Owen, 2008; Neuwirth and Paul, 2021), SimGrid enables controlled, repeatable failure injection and realistic end-to-end time accounting at systems that are impractical to reproduce experimentally such as a 600​k600\mathrm{k} H100 cluster (Casanova et al., 2014). Our simulators emulate SPARe+CKPT and compare it with replication with checkpointing (Rep+CKPT) and original Data Parallelism with checkpointing (CKPT-only) baselines under realistic system parameters projected for a 600​k600\mathrm{k} H100 cluster.

5.1 Realistic System Parameters

Table 1 shows system parameters we have set to emulate a restart-dominant system of 600​k600\mathrm{k} H100s, where MTBF is projected to be m=5m=5-min according to the scaling law validated by Kokolis et al. (2025) and MTBF reported for 16​k16\mathrm{k} H100s (Dubey et al., 2024). We set the global restart to take Tr=60T_{r}=60-min to test SPARe and baselines on a harsh restart-dominant regime. We set the LLM to be of 1010T parameters of memory size 20 TB (FP16). We consider three cases: dividing the cluster into (i) N=200N=200, (ii) N=600N=600, and (iii) N=1000N=1000 parallel groups. From the Llama 3 training report of Dubey et al. (2024) and Chu et al. (2025), we project the compute power per GPU to be 400400 TFLOPs and one shard of training data to be of size 4×64​M Tokens4\times 64\text{M Tokens}, considering 44 gradient accumulations. Consequently, we set the compute time per shard to be Tcomp=64​sT_{\text{comp}}=64\text{s}44 4 Regardless of NN, per GPU workload is the same 256​M Tokens400​TFLOPs\frac{256\text{M Tokens}}{400\text{TFLOPs}}.. We model the global all-reduce for gradient synchronization to be ring-based (Patarasuk and Yuan, 2009), hence scales up linearly by NN and take Ta=2,6,10​sT_{a}=2,6,10\text{s} for each NN considering the partial gradient size of 20​TB20\text{TB} and conservative collective goodput per GPU of 400400 Gb/s. Therefore, we set a training step that computes one data shard to take (Tcomp+Ta)(T_{\text{comp}}+T_{a}) for simplicity, and set 10,00010,000 steps to finish the training: the base time-to-train in the no-failure scenario is T0=10,000×(Tcomp+Ta)T_{0}=10,000\times(T_{\text{comp}}+T_{a}).

We inject failure events following a Weibull distribution (Weibull, 1951) to emulate real-world system behavior and choose the seminal shape parameter of k=0.78k=0.78 (Schroeder and Gibson, 2009). As we model a system that detects failed group(s) only at the global all-reduce step, we assume the failed all-reduce to take, in expectation, half the time of a successful one, without loss of generality.

Lastly, we set both partial recovery cost (shrink) and reordering controller cost to be 0.1​s0.1\text{s}, set checkpoint save time to be 11-min, calculate optimal checkpointing period Tc⋆T_{c}^{\star} from Eq. (1), and add jitter of normal distribution ×𝒩⁡(1,0.052)\times\mathcal{N}(1,0.05^{2}) to all events to reflect real-life variances and system noise.

5.2 Performance Evaluation Results

We created three event trails and ran each for three schemes of SPARe+CKPT, Rep+CKPT, and CKPT-only. See Appendix E for the flowchart of each scheme.

5.2.1 Results of Conventional Baselines

Under the harsh restart-dominant setting, CKPT-only did not proceed more than a few steps in a time where other schemes would finish the training. On the other hand, Rep+CKPT achieved minimal time-to-train at low redundancy r=3r=3 in all cases as shown in Fig. 6, consistent to prior works of Ferreira et al. (2011) and Elliott et al. (2012). For higher redundancies however, Fig. 6 clearly shows that the time-to-train of Rep+CKPT inflates linearly from the r×r\times overhead.

5.2.2 SPARe Results and Gain Analysis

SPARe+CKPT proves to fully exploit the significant availability (>90%>90\%) at high redundancies by keeping the computation overhead low (2∼3×2\sim 3\times) with failure-adaptive reordering . Fig. 6 shows the normalized time-to-train J⁡(r)=time-to-train/T0J(r)=\text{time-to-train}/T_{0} along with its theoretical prediction from J⁡(r)J(r) (7), and Fig. 7 shows empirical availability with theoretical projection A⋆​(μ​m)A^{\star}(\mu m) (2). SPARe+CKPT performs better than predicted at high redundancies, showing higher availability and clearly lower time-to-triain. That is because failure rate effectively decreases for high accumulation, as it is proportional to the number of active GPUs (Schroeder and Gibson, 2009; Kokolis et al., 2025); as high rr →\rightarrow high μ⁡(N,r)\mu(N,r), hence for higher rr and NN failure masking scheme is more advantageous. Fig. 8 shows the average number of stacks computed per training step, in other words, the empirical computation overhead along with its theoretical prediction of S¯​(N,r)\overline{S}(N,r) (5). Our formula closely fits the empirical values within ≤4%\leq 4\% absolute error, validating Thm. (4.2).

However, SPARe+CKPT performs worse than expected at low redundancies, even worse than Rep+CKPT at r=2r=2. Fig. 8 explicitly shows that the theoretical prediction S¯\overline{S} (5) still closely fits the simulations at low redundancies, indicating our theories on computation overhead are solid. Therefore, the deterioration comes from the k<1k<1 Weibull distribution, where failure accumulates faster at early accumulation: low rr →\rightarrow low μ⁡(N,r)\mu(N,r), hence system encounters the disruptive global restarts much more frequently than our predictions made upon exponential distribution. This implies that this issue does not set a fundamental limit on SPARe, and can be easily improved by employing dynamic-based checkpointing (Bougeret et al., 2011; Benoit et al., 2022) effective for Weibull distribution.

We evaluate the gain of SPARe+CKPT versus Rep+CKPT on the minimal time-to-train/T0/T_{0} achieved in each scheme and NN (Table 2). Compared to the best of Rep+CKPT, the best of SPARe+CKPT achieved 40∼50%40\sim 50\% gain in time-to-train. Note that the theoretical predictions of the optimal r⋆r^{\star} (8) for SPARe+CKPT are r⋆=8,10,10r^{\star}=8,10,10 at N=200,600,1000N=200,600,1000 in Thm. (4.3), showing slight discrepancies coming from the exponential distribution assumption: for low NN use SPARe with higher redundancy than r⋆r^{\star} (8), and for high NN use lower redundancy than r⋆r^{\star} (8).

6 Conclusion

In this work, we have introduced SPARe: Stacked Parallelism with Adaptive Reordering, which masks failures as many as traditional replication yet keeps the computation overhead as low as 2∼3×2\sim 3\times even for high redundancies. SPARe achieves substantially smaller time-to-train compared to traditional replication baseline, 40∼50%40\sim 50\% lower according to our realistic SimGrid-based discrete event simulations, at the harsh restart-dominant system setting projected for 600​k600\mathrm{k} H100 GPUs. In the imminent restart-dominant regime, masking failures, hence bypassing global restarts, is the most direct and intuitive strategy. SPARe positions itself as an effective and practical proposal for fault-tolerant LLM pretraining systems with 100​k+100\mathrm{k}+ GPUs.

Impact Statement

This work aims to advance fault-tolerant distributed training system on to the imminent restart-dominant regime, with the goal of achieving system availability over 90%90\% yet keeping computation overhead low to finish the training in practical time span. By substantially reducing the time-to-train required for next generation LLM pretraining, the proposed method of SPARe lowers the cost of frontier foundation model training and further elevate the ceiling for LLM scaling. More broadly, finishing foundation model training faster can contribute to lower energy consumption and more sustainable use of extreme scale HPC clusters. At the same time, increased accessibility to scale up LLM pretraining may accelerate progress of foundation model studies and development, impacting wide range of science and engineering. All experiments in this paper are conducted using publicly available libraries. The method itself is a fault-tolerance protocol for large parallel systems and does not introduce new capabilities that are inherently harmful. We do not foresee any immediate negative societal impacts directly resulting from this work.

B.1 Mathematical definition of SPARe

Definition B.1 (Cyclic Golomb Ruler distribution rule).

Set GrN={g0,…,gr−1}⊂ℤNG^{N}_{r}=\{g_{0},\dots,g_{r-1}\}\subset\mathbb{Z}_{N}55 5 ℤN:=ℤ/N​ℤ\mathbb{Z}_{N}:=\mathbb{Z}/N\mathbb{Z}, the additive cyclic group of integers modulo NN, i.e., residues {0,1,…,N−1}\{0,1,\dots,N-1\} with addition mod NN as the optimal Golomb Ruler (Golomb, 2017) of length rr, the set of unique pairwise differences modulo NN with g0=0g_{0}=0 and minimal gr−1g_{r-1}. In other words, the pairwise difference set {±(ga−gb)modN:0≤a<b≤r−1}\{\pm(g_{a}-g_{b})\bmod N:0\leq a<b\leq r-1\} has r⁡(r−1)r(r-1) distinct non-zero elements. A SPARe scheme (N,r)(N,r) distributes shards of type i∈[N]i\in[N] across NN groups with redundancy rr as:

Hi:={(i−g)modN:g∈GrN},H_{i}:=\{\,(i-g)\bmod N:g\in G^{N}_{r}\,\},\vskip-10.00002pt (10)

where HiH_{i} is the host set, set of group indices hosting shard ii, with the caveat of N≥(2​gr−1−1)N\geq(2g_{r-1}-1). Equivalently, each group ww hosts type set, set of shard indices group ww hosts:

Tw:={(w+g)modN:g∈GrN}.T_{w}:=\{\,(w+g)\bmod N:g\in G^{N}_{r}\,\}. (11)

We provide a lemma to prove that the cyclic Golomb Ruler distribution rule of Def. (B.1) achieves our intention.

Lemma B.2.

Following the cyclic Golomb Ruler distribution rule of Def. (B.1), any two distinct shard types of (N,r)(N,r) share at most one host: |Hi∩Hj|≤1​(i≠j)\lvert H_{i}\cap H_{j}\rvert\leq 1(i\neq j).

Proof.

Assume i≠ji\neq j share two hosts w1,w2w_{1},w_{2} (|Hi∩Hj|≥2\lvert H_{i}\cap H_{j}\rvert\geq 2). Then there would be distinct ga,gb,gc,gd∈GrNg_{a},g_{b},g_{c},g_{d}\in G^{N}_{r} which suffice w1≡i−ga≡j−gbw_{1}\equiv i-g_{a}\equiv j-g_{b} and w2≡i−gc≡j−gd(modN)w_{2}\equiv i-g_{c}\equiv j-g_{d}\pmod{N} from Eq. (10). That results as ga−gb≡gc−gd(modN)g_{a}-g_{b}\equiv g_{c}-g_{d}\pmod{N} which contradicts to definition of GrNG^{N}_{r}. ∎

B.2 Proof of Theorem 4.1

Proof.

Let FF be the failure count at first wipe-out and Pk:=Pr{F>k}P_{k}:=Pr\{F>k\}. Expanding Pr{F=k}=Pk−1−Pk\Pr\{F=k\}=P_{k-1}-P_{k}, expectation value of FF can be written as:

μ⁡(N,r):=𝔼⁡[F]=∑k=0N−1Pk.\mu(N,r):=\mathbb{E}[F]=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}P_{k}.\vskip-5.0pt (12)

Fix failure count k∈{0,1,…,N}k\in\{0,1,\dots,N\}. Conditional on exactly kk node failures, the failed set Bk:=Ukc⊂[N]B_{k}:=U_{k}^{c}\subset[N] is a uniformly random kk-subset of [N][N]. For each group w∈[N]w\in[N], define the exchangeable trials

Yw:=𝟏{w∈Bk}∈{0,1}.Y_{w}:=\mathbf{1}\{w\in B_{k}\}\in\{0,1\}. (13)

For each shard type i∈[N]i\in[N], define the wipe-out event and indicator

Ai(k):={Hi⊆Bk},Xi(k):=𝟏{Ai(k)}.A_{i}^{(k)}:=\{H_{i}\subseteq B_{k}\},\qquad X_{i}^{(k)}:=\mathbf{1}\{A_{i}^{(k)}\}. (14)

Let the number of wiped-out types after kk failures as:

pk:=𝔼⁡[Xi(k)]=Pr⁡(Hi⊆Bk)=(N−rk−r)(Nk)=(k)r(N)r,p_{k}:=\mathbb{E}[X_{i}^{(k)}]=\Pr(H_{i}\subseteq B_{k})=\frac{\binom{N-r}{k-r}}{\binom{N}{k}}=\frac{(k)_{r}}{(N)_{r}}, (17)

=(k)2​r−1(N)2​r−1,\displaystyle=\frac{(k)_{2r-1}}{(N)_{2r-1}}, (21)
q0​(k)\displaystyle q_{0}(k) :=Pr⁡(Xi(k)​Xj(k)=1∣ti​j=0)=(k)2​r(N)2​r,\displaystyle:=\Pr(X_{i}^{(k)}X_{j}^{(k)}=1\mid t_{ij}=0)=\frac{(k)_{2r}}{(N)_{2r}}, (22)

B.3 Proof of Theorem 4.2

Proof.

Let qk∈{0,1}q_{k}\in\{0,1\} denote the indicator that patch compute is needed on the (k+1)th(k+1)^{\text{th}} failure that takes the count from kk to k+1k+1. We approximate the average overhead before wipe-out by averaging over the per-step stacks as:

S⁡(N,r)≈1μ​∑k=0⌊μ⌋−1(𝔼⁡[S⁡(Uk)]+𝔼⁡[qk]),S(N,r)\;\approx\;\frac{1}{\mu}\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor\mu\rfloor-1}\Big(\mathbb{E}[S(U_{k})]+\mathbb{E}[q_{k}]\Big), (31)

where μ=𝔼⁡[F]\mu=\mathbb{E}[F] is the average failure count to the first wipe-out of Thm. (4.1).

First, we show 𝔼⁡[S⁡(Uk)]≈c⁡(k)\mathbb{E}[S(U_{k})]\approx c(k) with Hall’s Marriage Theorem (Hall, 1987). What we want to show is that for failure count kk that k≤μ⁡(N,r)k\leq\mu(N,r), the strict inequality S⁡(Uk)>c⁡(k)S(U_{k})>c(k) occurs with negligible probability.

Fix s:=c⁡(k)s:=c(k) and form the bipartite incidence graph between types and surviving groups: type ii is adjacent to group ww iff group ww is surviving and also hosting type ii (w∈Hi∩Ukw\in H_{i}\cap U_{k}). Allowing free reordering within each group means that a group can be assigned up to ss types over the first ss stacks. Equivalently, replicate each group w∈Ukw\in U_{k} into ss distinct copies (w,1),…,(w,s)(w,1),\dots,(w,s) and set

Li:=(Hi∩Uk)×[s]⊆Uk×[s],L_{i}\;:=\;(H_{i}\cap U_{k})\times[s]\;\subseteq\;U_{k}\times[s],

the set of all feasible slots to which type ii may be assigned (one of its surviving hosts, at one of the first ss stacks). Then S⁡(Uk)≤sS(U_{k})\leq s is equivalent to the existence of a complete system of distinct representatives (C.D.R.) for {Li}i∈[N]\{L_{i}\}_{i\in[N]}; mathematically explained, an injection that can be written as ϕ:[N]→Uk×[s]\phi:[N]\to U_{k}\times[s] such that ϕ⁡(i)∈Li\phi(i)\in L_{i} for all ii.

By Hall’s Marriage Theorem (Hall, 1987), such an injection exists if and only if for every E⊆[N]E\subseteq[N],

|E|≤|⋃i∈ELi|=s⋅|⋃i∈E(Hi∩Uk)|.|E|\;\leq\;\Big|\bigcup_{i\in E}L_{i}\Big|\;=\;s\cdot\Big|\bigcup_{i\in E}(H_{i}\cap U_{k})\Big|. (32)

Therefore S⁡(Uk)>sS(U_{k})>s implies that (32) fails for some witness EE. Let the set of groups hosting the subset EE of shard types as RR:

R:=⋃i∈A(Hi∩Uk)⊆Uk,b:=|R|.R:=\bigcup_{i\in A}(H_{i}\cap U_{k})\subseteq U_{k},\qquad b:=|R|.

Then |E|>s​|R||E|>s|R| and every i∈Ei\in E satisfies Hi∩Uk⊆RH_{i}\cap U_{k}\subseteq R. Define the number of shards that must be computed by groups in RR as CR​(k)C_{R}(k):

CR​(k):=|{i∈[N]:Hi∩Uk⊆R}|.C_{R}(k)\;:=\;\big|\{\,i\in[N]:H_{i}\cap U_{k}\subseteq R\,\}\big|.

We have the implication

{S(Uk)>s}⊆⋃R⊆Uk{CR(k)>s|R|},\{S(U_{k})>s\}\;\subseteq\;\bigcup_{R\subseteq U_{k}}\{C_{R}(k)>s|R|\}, (33)

which means that when RR is overloaded with too many number of shards (CR​(k)C_{R}(k)) it is mandated to compute, then Eq. (32) is to be violated hence S⁡(Uk)>c⁡(k)S(U_{k})>c(k).

Now we bound the RHS in Eq. (33) to formulate the cases where Eq. (32) is violated. Write x:=k/Nx:=k/N and recall that |Hi|=r|H_{i}|=r and, by Lem. (B.2), tmax≤1t_{\max}\leq 1.

Case 1. Single-group pinned overload (b=1b=1). First case S⁡(Uk)>c⁡(k)S(U_{k})>c(k) comes true (Eq. (32) violated), is when a group is mandated to compute certain shards; let us call it as the single-group pinned overload Ow​(k)O_{w}(k): For w∈Ukw\in U_{k} define the pinned load

Ow​(k):=|{i:Hi∩Uk={w}}|.O_{w}(k)\;:=\;\big|\{\,i:H_{i}\cap U_{k}=\{w\}\,\}\big|.

If Ow​(k)≥s+1O_{w}(k)\geq s+1 (OPENs:=c⁡(k))s:=c(k)), then R={w}R=\{w\} violates Eq. (33) hence Eq. (32). Conditional on w∈Ukw\in U_{k}, for any type i∈Twi\in T_{w} (group ww’s type set), ii is pinned to ww exactly when the other r−1r-1 hosts of ii all fail, hence

qk,N\displaystyle q_{k,N} :=Pr⁡(Hi∩Uk={w}∣w∈Uk)\displaystyle:=\Pr\!\left(H_{i}\cap U_{k}=\{w\}\mid w\in U_{k}\right)
=(k)r−1(N−1)r−1=xr−1(1+o(1))(k<N).\displaystyle=\frac{(k)_{r-1}}{(N-1)_{r-1}}=x^{r-1}(1+o(1))\quad(k<N). (34)

From Lem. (B.2) (tmax≤1t_{\max}\leq 1), a binomial tail bound for Ow​(k)O_{w}(k) is valid and a union bound over at most NN groups gives

Pr(∃w∈Uk:Ow(k)≥s+1)≤N(rs+1)qk,Ns+1.\Pr\big(\exists w\in U_{k}:O_{w}(k)\geq s+1\big)\;\leq\;N\binom{r}{s+1}q_{k,N}^{\,s+1}. (35)

On the first-wipe-out scale k≍μ=𝒪⁡(N1−1/r)k\asymp\mu=\mathcal{O}(N^{1-1/r}), we have x≍N−1/rx\asymp N^{-1/r} and hence qk,N≍N−(r−1)/rq_{k,N}\asymp N^{-(r-1)/r}, so the RHS of (35) behaves like N1−(s+1)​(r−1)/rN^{1-(s+1)(r-1)/r} up to constants, which vanishes for all fixed r≥2r\geq 2 and s=c⁡(k)≥2s=c(k)\geq 2. Thus Case 1 is negligible.

Case 2. Multi-group Hall witnesses (b≥2b\geq 2). Overload may not only happen to a single group, but on multiple groups as well. Fix R⊆UkR\subseteq U_{k} with |R|=b≥2|R|=b\geq 2. A type counted in CR​(k)C_{R}(k) must have all its surviving hosts inside RR. Such a type either (i) has exactly one surviving host in RR (it is pinned to some w∈Rw\in R), or (ii) has at least two surviving hosts in RR. Hence,

𝔼⁡[CR​(k)]≤r​b⋅qk,N+(b2)⋅(k)r−2(N−2)r−2.\mathbb{E}[C_{R}(k)]\;\leq\;rb\cdot q_{k,N}\;+\;\binom{b}{2}\cdot\frac{(k)_{r-2}}{(N-2)_{r-2}}. (36)

The first term counts pinned types across the r​brb types hosted by RR. For the second term, note that if two groups shared two distinct types, it contradicts tmax≤1t_{\max}\leq 1; hence each group-pair in RR can jointly host at most one type, and for such a type to have all other r−2r-2 hosts failed has probability at most (k)r−2/(N−2)r−2(k)_{r-2}/(N-2)_{r-2}.

For k≤μk\leq\mu we have x=𝒪(N−1/r)x=\mathcal{O}(N^{-1/r}), so both qk,Nq_{k,N} and (k)r−2/(N−2)r−2(k)_{r-2}/(N-2)_{r-2} vanish polynomially in NN, and in particular 𝔼⁡[CR​(k)]=o⁡(b)\mathbb{E}[C_{R}(k)]=o(b) uniformly over b≤mb\leq m. Since CR​(k)C_{R}(k) is a sum of indicators under sampling without replacement, a Chernoff bound (Chernoff, 1952; Hoeffding, 1963) applies and yields

Pr⁡(CR​(k)≥s​b)≤(e​𝔼​[CR​(k)]s​b)s​b=N−Ω⁡(b).\Pr\big(C_{R}(k)\geq sb\big)\;\leq\;\left(\frac{e\,\mathbb{E}[C_{R}(k)]}{sb}\right)^{sb}\;=\;N^{-\Omega(b)}. (37)

Union bounding Eq. (37) over all R⊆UkR\subseteq U_{k} and all bb implies

Pr⁡(S⁡(Uk)>s)=o⁡(1)for all ​k=0,1,…,⌊μ⌋−1.\Pr\big(S(U_{k})>s\big)=o(1)\qquad\text{for all }k=0,1,\dots,\lfloor\mu\rfloor-1.

Together with the deterministic lower bound S⁡(Uk)≥s=c⁡(k)S(U_{k})\geq s=c(k), we obtain

𝔼⁡[S⁡(Uk)]=c⁡(k)+o⁡(1)(k≤μ).\mathbb{E}[S(U_{k})]\;=\;c(k)+o(1)\qquad(k\leq\mu). (38)

Therefore, we show 𝔼⁡[S⁡(Uk)]≈c⁡(k)\mathbb{E}[S(U_{k})]\approx c(k). Now we compute the expectation value of the number of patch computes.

Fix kk and set s:=c⁡(k)s:=c(k), and set nkn_{k} as

nk=c⁡(k)​(N−k),n_{k}\;=\;c(k)(N-k), (39)

the number of stacks of computation before the all-reduce attempt. Let did_{i} be the number of how many type ii appears among the nkn_{k} slots; then di≥1d_{i}\geq 1 and ∑i=0N−1di=nk\sum_{i=0}^{N-1}d_{i}=n_{k}. Let uk:=|{i:di=1}|u_{k}:=|\{i:d_{i}=1\}| be the number of singleton types: types that appear exactly once among the nkn_{k} slots. Since every non-singleton types appear in nkn_{k} slots at least 22,

nk\displaystyle n_{k} =∑idi≥uk+2​(N−uk)=2​N−uk\displaystyle=\sum_{i}d_{i}\;\geq\;u_{k}+2(N-u_{k})=2N-u_{k}
⟹uk≥max⁡{0,2​N−nk}.\displaystyle\Longrightarrow u_{k}\;\geq\;\max\{0,2N-n_{k}\}.

As each singleton type corresponds to exactly one slot, when the newly failed group is removed, the ss slots computed by that group in the current step are lost, and patch-compute is needed iff at least one of those lost slots was singleton.

Define the singleton-slot fraction as

ρk:=max⁡{0,2​N−nk}nk.\rho_{k}\;:=\;\frac{\max\{0,2N-n_{k}\}}{n_{k}}. (40)

Under SPARe’s minimal movement reordering by MCMF algorithm (Goldberg and Tarjan, 1990), the singleton slots are typically packed, correlated across groups rather than scattered independently across the ss slots of each group. Hence the probability that a uniformly random newly failed group hits at least one singleton is well-approximated to first order by the singleton-slot fraction itself:

Pr⁡(patch compute at failure​k)≈ρk.\Pr(\text{patch compute at failure}\;k)\;\approx\;\rho_{k}. (41)

Therefore, substituting (38) and (41) into (31) yields

S¯​(N,r)≈1⌊μ⌋​∑k=0⌊μ⌋−1(c⁡(k)+ρk),\overline{S}(N,r)\;\approx\;\frac{1}{\lfloor\mu\rfloor}\sum_{k=0}^{\lfloor\mu\rfloor-1}\left(c(k)+\rho_{k}\right),

with nk=c⁡(k)​(N−k)n_{k}=c(k)(N-k) and ρk=max⁡{0,2​N−nk}/nk\rho_{k}=\max\{0,2N-n_{k}\}/n_{k}, proving Thm. (4.2). ∎

B.4 Proof of Theorem 4.3

Proof.

Recall that the normalized time-to-train of SPARe+CKPT is Eq. (7)

J⁡(r):=time-to-trainT0=S¯​(N,r)A⋆​(μ​(N,r)​m)J(r)\;:=\;\frac{\text{time-to-train}}{T_{0}}\;=\;\frac{\overline{S}(N,r)}{A^{\star}(\mu(N,r)\,m)} (42)

where mm is the MTBF between node failures, μ⁡(N,r)\mu(N,r) is the average failure count to first wipe-out from Thm. (4.1), and A⋆​(⋅)A^{\star}(\cdot) is the maximal availability obtained by the optimal CKPT period of Eq. (1),(2).

Note that the patch term in S¯​(N,r)\overline{S}(N,r) (5) is always bounded:

0≤ 1−(1−ρk)c⁡(k)≤ 1,0\;\leq\;1-(1-\rho_{k})^{c(k)}\;\leq\;1, (43)

from 0≤ρk≤10\leq\rho_{k}\leq 1. Therefore, the capacity term 𝔼⁡[S⁡(Uk)]≈c⁡(k)\mathbb{E}[S(U_{k})]\approx c(k) dominates S¯\overline{S}, which increases as a step-function:

c⁡(k)=2for​ 1≤k≤N2,\displaystyle c(k)=2\ \ \text{for}\ \ 1\leq k\leq\frac{N}{2},
c⁡(k)=3forN2<k≤2​N3,\displaystyle c(k)=3\ \ \text{for}\ \ \frac{N}{2}<k\leq\frac{2N}{3},
c⁡(k)=4for2​N3<k≤3​N4,\displaystyle c(k)=4\ \ \text{for}\ \ \frac{2N}{3}<k\leq\frac{3N}{4},

and so on. Thus, as long as the wipe-out threshold μ⁡(N,r)\mu(N,r) is below N/2N/2, the 𝔼⁡[S⁡(Uk)]\mathbb{E}[S(U_{k})] contribution in (5) stays pinned at ≈2\approx 2, and the only variation in S¯​(N,r)\overline{S}(N,r) comes from the bounded patch term (43). Once μ⁡(N,r)\mu(N,r) exceeds N/2N/2, a nontrivial fraction of indices kk in the sum (5) satisfy k>N/2k>N/2, forcing c⁡(k)≥3c(k)\geq 3 and thereby increasing S¯​(N,r)\overline{S}(N,r) by an Ω⁡(1)\Omega(1) amount while the patch term is bounded ≤1\leq 1: the increase rate of the numerator of J⁡(r)J(r) (7): S¯​(N,r)\overline{S}(N,r) (5), jumps up after k>N2k>\frac{N}{2}.

Now we look at the denominator of J⁡(r)J(r) (7): A⋆​(μ​m)A^{\star}(\mu m) (2). Because A⋆​(Tf)A^{\star}(T_{f}) increases monotonic in TfT_{f}, and Tf=μ⁡(N,r)​mT_{f}=\mu(N,r)m, increasing rr (μ⁡(N,r)\mu(N,r) increases monotonic by rr) improves the denominator in (7).

On the other hand, (5) shows that S¯​(N,r)\overline{S}(N,r) remains of constant order ≈2+o⁡(1)\approx 2+o(1) until the first capacity bump at μ⁡(N,r)≈N/2\mu(N,r)\approx N/2, after which S¯​(N,r)\overline{S}(N,r) must increase because c⁡(k)c(k) becomes 33 for an increasing fraction of kk. Therefore, the minimizer of J⁡(r)J(r) occurs at the smallest redundancy rr that pushes μ⁡(N,r)\mu(N,r) to this first capacity transition,

μ⁡(N,r⋆)≈N2,\mu(N,r^{\star})\;\approx\;\frac{N}{2}, (44)

since below r⋆r^{\star} one can still increase availability without paying the c⁡(k)≥3c(k)\geq 3 penalty on S¯​(N,r)\overline{S}(N,r).

Now we solve μ⁡(N,r⋆)≈N2\mu(N,r^{\star})\;\approx\;\frac{N}{2} to find optimal redundancy r⋆r^{\star} that minimizes J⁡(r)J(r). Let ε:=1/r\varepsilon:=1/r and rewrite μ⁡(N,r)\mu(N,r) (3) as

μ⁡(N,r)N=Γ⁡(ε)​ε​N−ε.\frac{\mu(N,r)}{N}=\Gamma(\varepsilon)\,\varepsilon\,N^{-\varepsilon}.

Imposing μ⁡(N,r⋆)≈N2\mu(N,r^{\star})\;\approx\;\frac{N}{2} gives

Γ⁡(ε)​ε​N−ε≈12.\Gamma(\varepsilon)\,\varepsilon\,N^{-\varepsilon}\;\approx\;\frac{1}{2}. (45)

For ε≪1\varepsilon\ll 1, we use the standard expansion

Γ⁡(ε)=1ε−γ+𝒪⁡(ε),\Gamma(\varepsilon)\;=\;\frac{1}{\varepsilon}-\gamma+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon),

where γ≈0.57721\gamma\approx 0.57721 is the Euler-Mascheroni constant (NIST, 2025). Multiplying by ε\varepsilon yields

Γ⁡(ε)​ε= 1−γ​ε+𝒪⁡(ε2).\Gamma(\varepsilon)\,\varepsilon\;=\;1-\gamma\varepsilon+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{2}).

Substituting into (45) and taking logarithms,

log⁡(1−γ​ε+𝒪⁡(ε2))−ε​log⁡N≈−log⁡2.\log\!\bigl(1-\gamma\varepsilon+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{2})\bigr)\;-\;\varepsilon\log N\;\approx\;-\log 2.

Using log⁡(1−x)=−x+𝒪⁡(x2)\log(1-x)=-x+\mathcal{O}(x^{2}) gives

−(γ+log⁡N)​ε+O⁡(ε2)≈−log⁡2,-(\gamma+\log N)\,\varepsilon+O(\varepsilon^{2})\;\approx\;-\log 2,

hence

ε≈log⁡2log⁡N+γ⟹r⋆=1ε≈log⁡N+γlog⁡2\displaystyle\varepsilon\;\approx\;\frac{\log 2}{\log N+\gamma}\Longrightarrow r^{\star}=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\approx\frac{\log N+\gamma}{\log 2}
=log2⁡N+γln⁡2.\displaystyle=\log_{2}N\;+\;\frac{\gamma}{\ln 2}.

Finally, since rr is an integer, we take the nearest-integer (or floor) version:

r⋆≈⌊log2⁡N+γln⁡2⌋≈⌊log2⁡N+0.833⌋,r^{\star}\;\approx\;\Bigl\lfloor\log_{2}N+\frac{\gamma}{\ln 2}\Bigr\rfloor\;\approx\;\bigl\lfloor\log_{2}N+0.833\bigr\rfloor,

proving Thm. (4.3). ∎

Appendix C Monte-Carlo Simulation Results

Table 4 (N=200N=200), Table 5 (N=600N=600), Table 6 (N=1000N=1000) show the Monte-Carlo simulation results on the average failure count μ⁡(N,r)\mu(N,r) (3), and the expectation value of all-reduce stack each scheme with 1,0001,000 trials. Columns of red color are the theoretical values from the formula Eq. (3) and Eq. (6), and the black colored are the simulation results. The results are highly consistent with Thm. (4.1) and Thm. (4.2): Across N∈{200,600,1000}N\in\{200,600,1000\} and all tested redundancies, Monte Carlo results match the closed-form formulas with Mean Absolute Percentage Error 1.13%1.13\% for μ⁡(N,r)\mu(N,r), and 0.60%0.60\% for average all-reduce stack, with correlations ≥0.996\geq 0.996 (worst-case relative error ≤5.06%\leq 5.06\%). See the file reordering.ipynb in Supplementary Materials for the code and the detailed simulation results. Simulation is implemented by emulating the trails of random independent failures and corresponding reordering events before the first wipe-out.

Appendix D Reordering Controller Algorithm

We detail how HK-FIXED and HK-FREE (Hopcroft and Karp, 1973), and MCMF (Goldberg and Tarjan, 1990) implement Alg. (2), reordering controller, and why their costs are negligible at N∼𝒪⁡(102−3)N\sim\mathcal{O}(10^{2-3}).

Bipartite feasibility model.

Define a bipartite graph with left vertices ℒ=[N]\mathcal{L}=[N] (types) and right vertices ℛ=Uk×[SA]\mathcal{R}=U_{k}\times[S_{A}] (slots of computation among survivors). An edge (i,(w,t))(i,(w,t)) means survivor ww can compute type ii at stack tt. A size-NN matching is equivalent to collecting all NN types by depth SAS_{A} (one type per slot, every type covered).

HK-FIXED (Phase 0: validate committed stacks).

Given the committed depth SAS_{A} and the current per-group order stk⁡[w]\mathrm{stk}[w], construct edges (stk​[w]​[t],(w,t))(\mathrm{stk}[w][t],(w,t)) for all w∈Ukw\in U_{k}, t≤SAt\leq S_{A}. Run Hopcroft–Karp (Hopcroft and Karp, 1973) to test if the maximum matching has size NN. If yes, all-reduce at SAS_{A} succeeds without reordering; otherwise proceed to Phase 1.

HK-FREE (Phase 1: find minimal S⁡(Uk)S(U_{k}) under free reordering).

For candidate S=SA,SA+1,…,rS=S_{A},S_{A}+1,\dots,r, allow free permutation within each group stack: add edges (i,(w,t))(i,(w,t)) iff w∈Hi∩Ukw\in H_{i}\cap U_{k}. Run Hopcroft–Karp (Hopcroft and Karp, 1973); the first SS with matching size NN is S⁡(Uk)S(U_{k}). If no S≤rS\leq r works, some type(s) has no surviving host (wipe-out) and the controller restarts.

MCMF (Phase 2: minimum-movement reordering at S⁡(Uk)S(U_{k})).

At S⋆:=S⁡(Uk)S^{\star}:=S(U_{k}), we seek a feasible assignment that changes stacks minimally. Use the same bipartite graph but assign each edge a movement cost as 00 if already at position tt, 11 if making a movement. Compute a min-cost size-NN assignment via a standard min cost max flow algorithm (Goldberg and Tarjan, 1990), then update each survivors’ stack accordingly.

Complexity and latency.

Hopcroft–Karp (Hopcroft and Karp, 1973) runs in 𝒪⁡(E​V)\mathcal{O}(E\sqrt{V}) time where EE is the number of edges and VV is the number of vertexes (nodes). Here V=N+(N−k)​SV=N+(N-k)S and E≤N⋅r⋅SE\leq N\cdot r\cdot S, since each type has ≤r\leq r surviving hosts and SS slots to be assigned per each group. For N∼𝒪⁡(102−3)N\sim\mathcal{O}(10^{2-3}) and r≤𝒪⁡(100−1)r\leq\mathcal{O}(10^{0-1}), and S≈2S\approx 2–33, these graphs are sparse and small, so HK-FIXED/HK-FREE are sub-100ms in compiled implementations. MCMF is run only upon failures and restricted to types and slots impacted by the failure, making its practical cost likewise negligible; we conservatively model the controller as 0.10.1s overhead per failure in our simulations.
